I am 50 this year, and I have been farming this 10.9 mu for 20 years. I finished primary school, so I can read the numbers on the fertilizer bags and do the math for how many bags I need. My husband and son work in a factory in town and send money home, but I am the one who decides what happens on the land. My daughter-in-law helps me when it gets busy.

For winter wheat, I plant right after National Day, around October 8th. Last year I used Luyuan 502 and got about 950 jin per mu, but my neighbor Lao Wang used Jimai 22 and got over 1000 jin. This year I am switching to Jimai 22 — it costs a bit more for seed, about 45 yuan per mu, but if everyone around me is getting better yield, I should too. I never save my own wheat seed; it does not grow as strong.

For wheat fertilizer, I do what I did last year. Before sowing, I spread one full bag of compound fertilizer per mu — 50 kg, the one that says 15-15-15 on the bag. That gives me 7.5 kg of nitrogen, 7.5 kg of phosphate, and 7.5 kg of potash per mu. Then in late March, when the wheat turns green, I topdress with half a bag of urea per mu, about 25 kg. That is another 11.5 kg of nitrogen. So altogether about 19 kg nitrogen per mu. The extension poster at the village office says 15 kg is enough, but three years ago I tried cutting back and the wheat turned yellow and thin. I would rather waste a little fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. Buying flour from the market costs more than an extra bag of urea.

I have a well, so I irrigate wheat three times: once before winter so the seedlings do not freeze, once at jointing in April, and once at grain filling in May. Each time costs about 15 yuan per mu for the electricity to run the pump. It adds up, but dry wheat means empty heads.

For pesticides on wheat, I spray three times: herbicide once after sowing to kill the weeds, insecticide once in spring when the aphids come, and fungicide once if I see rust on the leaves. Last year I did all three, and it cost about 80 yuan per mu total, but without it I would have lost much more.

For summer maize, there is no time to rest after wheat harvest in early June. The rain is coming, and if I wait more than five days the soil dries out. I hire the seeding machine to drill the maize directly into the wheat stubble — no-tillage. It saves diesel and time, and the stubble keeps some moisture. Everyone in the village uses Deng Hai 605 hybrid seed. It is 120 yuan for a 5-jin bag, and one bag covers about 3 mu, so that is 40 yuan per mu.

For maize fertilizer, at sowing I put down 40 kg of compound fertilizer per mu, again 15-15-15. That is 6 kg each of nitrogen, phosphate, and potash. Then at the big trumpet stage in July, I spread 20 kg of urea per mu, which is about 9 kg more nitrogen. Total nitrogen is about 15 kg per mu. Two years ago I put 50 kg compound and 25 kg urea, and the stalks grew too tall and lodged in a windstorm. So I cut back a little, and last year it stood fine. I learned my lesson.

Maize gets summer rain, but some years July is dry. I plan to irrigate twice if needed — once at jointing and once at filling. Last year I watered twice, and the yield was good. If it rains enough, maybe once is enough, but I budget for two.

For maize pesticides, I spray herbicide once before sowing, and insecticide twice — once for corn borer in July and once for armyworm if they show up in August. That is three applications.

I expect my wheat to give me about 500 kg per mu, and my maize about 600 kg per mu. If both do well, that is over 11,000 kg total — enough for my family to eat and to sell the surplus. I am not changing much this year. Last year was decent, and change is risky when you have a family to feed.
